sim00_boundary_full.caption: SIM-0 disruption boundary: dv_shift, design specific energy, safe intercept-velocity ceiling and the self-disposal floor, for every (h, dh, beta, Es_c).

sim00_headline.caption: Design point at beta=1.5, gamma=2, Es_c=40 kJ/kg, dh=200 km, v_rel=619 m/s (plan Part 1.4 layout, recomputed).

sim00_vmax_safe.caption: Safe intercept-velocity ceiling vs altitude. Everything below a solid line is sub-catastrophic; below the dashed line it stays sub-catastrophic with the γ=2 mass margin. The dotted line is the minimum v_rel that guarantees missed projectile mass is on an immediate-reentry trajectory.

sim00_pivot_headline.caption: Design-point specific energy for direct reentry (v4) versus the 200 km accelerated-reentry shift (v5) at a common intercept velocity. The v5 design point is sub-catastrophic at every altitude and for every β in the envelope.

sim01_mass_scaling_full.caption: Momentum-balance projectile mass on target, f(h), and the consistency check E_s < E_s,c, over (h, beta, v_rel, d_debris).

sim01_design_point.caption: 1 cm Al-6061 sphere (AM-2), v_rel = 619 m/s, dh = 200 km, gamma = 2.

sim01_f_of_h.caption: Required projectile mass on target per unit debris mass. Bands span the unvalidated β envelope. v5 needs 1.5–6× less mass than v4 at the same intercept velocity, and the advantage grows with altitude because dv_shift falls while dv_direct rises.

sim01_grain_size.caption: Diameter of a single compact projectile carrying the full design mass. Rhenium's 9% density advantage over tungsten changes the diameter by only 3%.

sim02_decay_full.caption: Pre- and post-kick orbital lifetime for solid Al-6061 spheres, orbit-averaged Gauss propagation on real NRLMSISE-00 density.

sim02_altitude_ceilings.caption: Highest starting altitude at which a single Delta-h kick puts the object inside the 25-yr and 5-yr disposal rules.

sim02_staged_kicks.caption: Number of successive sub-catastrophic 200 km kicks needed to bring an object inside the 25-yr rule. The single-kick altitude ceiling is where this first exceeds one.

sim02_missed_mass_fate.caption: Fate of projectile mass that misses. A retrograde intercept at v_rel > dv_direct leaves the missed mass on a sub-orbital trajectory that reenters on its first perigee pass; the counterfactual column is the v4 assumption of a grain left on the original circular orbit.

sim02_lifetime_vs_altitude.caption: Post-kick orbital lifetime against pre-kick altitude for five debris sizes and three solar activity cases. Crossings of the 25-yr and 5-yr lines are the altitude ceilings.

sim03_cw_vs_ballistic.caption: Exact Clohessy-Wiltshire cloud spreading versus straight-line ballistic spreading at engagement times-of-flight.

sim03_cw_long_timescale.caption: CW evolution of a 10 mm/s dispersion at 800 km over release-to-intercept times from 1 s to one orbit (context: shows where CW departs from ballistic, and that the engagement does not operate there).

sim03_sigma_cloud_export.caption: MANDATED EXPORT to SIM-4: cloud cross-section sigma_cloud at the exact times-of-flight used for R = 1, 5, 10, 50, 100 m, with the delivered-mass fraction for a perfectly centred shot.

sim03_pareto_mass_penalty.caption: Launched-mass penalty versus tolerated miss distance for a 1 cm target, with the optimal cloud sigma. The closed-form column is the small-target limit  pi*e*d_miss^2/A_t.

sim03_grain_mode.caption: Grain-size selection: number of grains striking a 1 cm target, Poisson variability of the delivered momentum, and per-impact specific energy. Design mass on target 0.161 g (800 km, beta=1.5, v_rel=619 m/s).

sim03_mass_penalty.caption: Launched-mass penalty as a function of the miss distance the shot pattern must tolerate. The penalty is quadratic in miss distance and inversely proportional to target cross-section, which is why cost per object rises steeply for the smallest debris.

sim03_sigma_cloud.caption: Cloud cross-section at intercept. Because time-of-flight is R/v_rel, the pattern size is set by the ratio of transverse dispersion to intercept velocity times range — a launcher design choice, tunable to match the achievable miss distance.

sim04_error_budget_full.caption: Terminal error budget under three miss models, with the launched-mass penalty each implies at 90% delivery confidence. p_hit_plan_* columns apply the plan's Bernoulli model at the v4 cloud size (sigma=0.38 m) for direct comparability.

sim04_headline_design_case.caption: R = 10 m, u = 10 m/s, pointing 200 urad, muzzle dispersion 0.1%, 100 MHz ranging, v_rel = 619 m/s, 1 cm target.

sim04_miss_vs_tau.caption: Miss distance against control-loop latency. Under the v4 model the miss grows as v_rel*tau and passes metres by 10 ms. Under the co-orbital extrapolating budget the lag term is u*tau at most and the total is dominated by lag-independent launcher pointing.

sim04_mass_vs_range.caption: Launched mass per engagement at 90% delivery confidence. Because the dominant miss term is proportional to range, closing to short range is worth more than any improvement in control latency.

sim05_fragmentation_full.caption: Fragment production under the NASA SBM (regime-selected effective mass, AM-13) and under an energy-based cratering bound, across altitude, beta, intercept velocity and the catastrophic-threshold range.

tags.calibration: SBM extrapolated below its fit velocity

sim05_swarm_per_impact.caption: AM-16: per-impact specific energy for the swarm. Reported ALWAYS alongside the bulk figure, never instead of it. The bulk (single-impactor) energy at the v5 design point is already sub-catastrophic, so this branch is a robustness reserve, not a load-bearing assumption.

sim05_net_debris_ledger.caption: Net debris per engagement at 800 km. 'SBM branch' applies the mandated model verbatim; 'physical' recognises that a sub-catastrophic impact cannot liberate a fragment larger than the target it did not disrupt.

sim05_es_vs_vrel.caption: Bulk specific energy against intercept velocity. The design point sits at roughly half the catastrophic threshold; the margin closes at high v_rel and low beta, which is what sets the velocity ceiling used in SIM-13.

sim06_demonstrated_benchmarks.caption: Demonstrated electromagnetic-launch benchmarks (AM-9: no aspirational systems).

sim06_coilgun_designs.caption: Coilgun sizing across the projectile mass/velocity grid: barrel length at a 10,000 g acceleration limit, stage count, stored electrical energy, capacitor and copper mass.

sim06_gap_analysis.caption: Required muzzle energy versus the largest demonstrated electromagnetic launch.

sim06_envelope.caption: Required launcher operating point against demonstrated electromagnetic launches. The v5 requirement sits far inside hardware that already exists, which is a direct consequence of the reduced Delta-v and the low intercept velocity the energy gate prefers.

sim07_material_comparison.caption: Material comparison on the metrics that actually differentiate: momentum per unit mass (identical), delivered cost, supply, missed-grain area-to-mass, ablation energy, oxide behaviour.

sim07_supply_ceiling.caption: Engagements per year supportable at 1% of world production.

sim07_weighted_ranking.caption: Weighted ranking. Weights stated explicitly: delivered cost 0.35, supply 0.25, missed-grain persistence 0.20, environmental 0.20, momentum 0.00 (identical across materials).

sim07_material_trade.caption: Material cost and supply. Because momentum transfer is density-independent, these are the axes that actually discriminate, and rhenium loses both.

sim08_ablation.caption: Ablated mass fraction against particle size. Small grains survive because they decelerate high and radiate efficiently; they are nonetheless harmless, carrying microjoules of impact energy at terminal velocity.

sim08_thermal_sensitivity.caption: Sensitivity of the ablated fraction to the two UNVALIDATED thermal inputs: effective heat of ablation (3.5-5.5 MJ/kg) and surface emissivity (0.2-0.6), for rhenium grains.

sim08_casualty.caption: Ground-casualty expectation per surviving fragment. The 15 J kinetic-energy threshold is the conventional serious-injury criterion used in NASA/FAA debris-casualty analysis; 0.36 m^2 is the standard mean human projected area.

sim08_deposition.caption: Annual metal deposition from the programme versus the natural cosmic-dust influx (~40,000 t/yr).

sim09_cost_full.caption: Full cost model: per-object and per-kg cost across debris size, altitude, beta, guidance budget, material, launch price, platform cost and engagement count.

sim09_cost_breakdown.caption: Cost breakdown per 1 cm object removed at 800 km, design guidance budget, rhenium at 2026 spot, $3000/kg launch, $50M platform amortised over 10,000 engagements.

sim09_competitors.caption: Side-by-side with published competitor costs. Per-object columns convert the per-kg figures using a 1 cm Al sphere (1.414 g) so the two conventions can be compared directly.

sim09_engagement_sensitivity.caption: Cost per object versus the number of engagements a platform completes in its life. Because consumables are ~$31 per object and platform amortisation is everything else, the engagement count is the single dominant economic variable -- and it is the one this study does not model (SIM-11 caveat, R10).

sim09_cost.caption: Cost per kg and per object removed. The mass penalty scales as sigma_miss^2/A_target, so cost per object falls with better guidance and cost per kg falls steeply with target size.

sim10_compliance_matrix.caption: Compliance matrix per altitude, debris size and solar case. Released-material tests are the binding licence conditions; target-lifetime tests are mission-effectiveness benchmarks.

sim10_transient_hazard.caption: Transient conjunction hazard of released material during its single descending pass through LEO, before reentry.

sim10_aviation.caption: Reentry timing and footprint for released material, and the resulting aviation hazard.

sim11_mass_budget.caption: FG01 mass budget. Power at 5 kW and 30 W/kg; structure 20% of subtotal; payload is the rhenium magazine.

sim11_recoil.caption: Recoil impulse from firing and the propellant needed to hold the operating orbit. Each shot pushes FG01 prograde because the projectile is fired retrograde.

sim11_plane_access.caption: Time to change orbital plane using differential nodal regression instead of propellant. Near-polar inclinations precess slowly, so plane access is slowest exactly where sun-synchronous debris concentrates.

sim11_end_of_life.caption: End-of-life options: controlled deorbit versus return to a 400 km reload hub.

sim12_viability.caption: P(viable) and per-constraint satisfaction probability by altitude, debris size and solar case, under both the plan-form and design-form guidance constraints.

sim12_convergence.caption: Monte-Carlo convergence at the highest-probability cell (0.5 cm debris, 900 km, nominal solar).

sim12_sobol.caption: Sobol indices for the design-form viability indicator at 0.5 cm, nominal solar (altitude sampled).

sim12_posteriors.caption: Posterior 5th/50th/95th percentiles at the best cell (0.5 cm, 900 km, nominal solar).

sim12_p_viable.caption: Joint probability that all five viability constraints hold. The two panels differ only in how the guidance constraint is defined, which is the single largest modelling choice in the study.

sim12_binding_constraints.caption: Per-constraint satisfaction probability against altitude. The lowest curve at each altitude is the binding constraint.

sim13_operating_grid.caption: Full design grid with epistemic-only Monte Carlo. Design variables fixed at R=10 m, 200 urad pointing, u=10 m/s, tau=10 ms, 0.1% muzzle dispersion.

sim13_top_operating_points.caption: Top 30 operating points ranked by P(viable) at nominal solar activity, with the solar-min and solar-max values alongside.

sim13_binding_constraints.caption: Binding-constraint ledger at the optimum. The lowest probability is the concept's true weak point.

sim13_engagement_conditional.caption: P(viable) against the number of objects one platform services in its life. This single quantity, which the study does not derive from first principles, carries the largest share of the residual uncertainty.

sim13_robustness.caption: Degradation of P(viable) as each design variable drifts from its chosen value, all else held.

sim13_operating_point.caption: Viability at the selected design configuration. The star marks the optimum. Viability falls above ~900 km because the decay gate fails, and below because nothing changes but cost keeps accruing.

int00_validation_3d.caption: Closed-form |w| and retrograde efficiency checked against explicit 3-D inertial states at a common node.

int00_kinematics.caption: Retrograde efficiency and disruption cost versus approach geometry. A crossing engagement wastes all but sin(θ/2) of its relative velocity on a useless cross-track impulse while paying the full |w|² in specific energy, so it exceeds the catastrophic threshold at every plane angle.

int00_crossing_energy_cost.caption: Projectile mass and specific energy required to deliver the SAME 51.8 m/s retrograde kick to a 1 cm target, as a function of approach geometry.

int00_combined_geometry.caption: The operational case: a nearly-co-orbital platform whose plane differs from the target's by theta. Specific energy for a fixed retrograde kick grows as 1 + (v_geom/v_launch)^2.

int00_guidance_sweep.caption: Miss distance vs. approach geometry, engagement range and control latency, under a no-lead and a lead-computing aim law.

int00_timeline.caption: Engagement window: how long a target of a given transverse rate remains inside tracking range.

int00_no_lead_cone.caption: The honest boundary: maximum transverse rate (and equivalent plane angle) for which a NON-extrapolating aim law still lands inside a 1 cm target.

int00_miss_vs_transverse.caption: Miss distance under a non-extrapolating aim law against target transverse rate. In the co-orbital regime the miss stays inside the target at every latency tested; the latency term only bites for geometries that INT-0 Part A has already excluded.

int01_validation_montecarlo.caption: Closed-form mass efficiency (non-central chi-square) against a grain-by-grain Monte-Carlo overlap count. Sample size is scaled per case so each MC estimate has >=2000 expected hits; the 'sigmas_from_mc' column is the discrepancy in units of the MC's own standard error, which is the meaningful test.

int01_areal_density.caption: Mass efficiency and grain count on target versus cloud diameter. A wider cloud is more forgiving of aim error but wastes mass as the square of its diameter; the 100-grain floor sets the largest usable grain size.

int02_beta_vs_velocity.caption: Momentum enhancement from crater-ejecta scaling. beta_low/high span mu in [0.40, 0.55] and k in [0.2, 0.5]. The oblique column applies <cos i> = 2/3 for a parallel beam on a curved target.

int02_mass_impact.caption: Consequence of the corrected beta for the mass budget at the SIM-13 optimum (1 cm target, 900 km, v_rel = 619 m/s).

int02_penetration.caption: Grain penetration depth (Poncelet form), crater volume and ejecta mass per grain. 'Perforates' compares against a 1 cm solid target.

int02_beta.caption: Momentum enhancement from crater-ejecta scaling. Below roughly three times the target's strength velocity almost nothing is ejected fast enough to add momentum, so β approaches its physical floor of 1. The v5 envelope, drawn from hypervelocity data, was too generous for this regime.

int03_launch_mass.caption: Launched mass, incident mass, bulk and per-grain specific energy across altitude, intercept velocity, cloud diameter and the INT-2 beta cases.

int03_am16_bulk_vs_pergrain.caption: AM-16 discharged: bulk specific energy and per-grain specific energy reported together. The swarm split is now computed from the resolved cloud, not assumed.

int03_dv_distribution.caption: Distribution of imparted Delta-v across shots, including aim scatter and Poisson swarm lumpiness. Replaces the deterministic single value used in v5 SIM-2.

int04_aim_tolerance.caption: Launched mass versus cloud diameter at fixed shot reliability, showing the interior optimum, and the resulting mass penalty against aim error compared with the v5 closed form.

int03_velocity_ceiling.caption: Velocity ceiling recomputed with the INT-2 beta. The v6 plan's proposed 1000-1100 m/s operating point is evaluated here.

int05_ejecta.caption: Cumulative ejecta size distribution per engagement. Production terminates at the crater diameter (0.4 mm), an order of magnitude below the 1 cm trackable threshold, so the engagement cannot create a trackable fragment through cratering.

int05_ejecta_decay.caption: Orbital lifetime of crater ejecta on the post-kick orbit (900 x 700 km), against the parent 1 cm fragment.

int05_net_debris.caption: Net-debris ledger at the 5 cm-cloud design point, separated by size threshold. The >1 cm line is the regulatory metric; the >1 mm line is reported for completeness and is not netted against the removal because sub-mm particles are not tracked objects and decay within two years.

int06_size_scaling.caption: Interception efficiency, launched mass and the figure of merit (kg removed per kg launched) against target size.

int06_drag_vs_size.caption: Drag force versus drag deceleration against target size. Decay is governed by the latter, which falls as 1/diameter.

int06_ballistic_coefficient.caption: Effect of the engagement on the target's own ballistic coefficient: embedded rhenium adds mass, crater ejecta removes it. Net effect on post-kick lifetime.

int06_staged_large_objects.caption: Kicks needed to bring an object at 900 km inside the 25-yr rule, and the resulting total projectile mass as a fraction of target mass. The '14% law' applies to ONE kick; large objects need several because their area-to-mass is far lower.

int06_target_size.caption: Interception efficiency, the mass figure of merit, and drag scaling against target size. Interception rises and saturates at a few centimetres; the figure of merit caps at βv_rel/(γΔv); drag deceleration falls as 1/diameter, so large objects decay more slowly.

eco02_cloud_spread.caption: How far each real breakup cloud has spread under differential J2 nodal regression since its event.

eco02_engageable.caption: Instantaneously engageable >=1 cm members per cluster, inside the INT-0 plane cone and an altitude band.

eco02_flux.caption: Engagement opportunities over a mission: members already in the plane cone plus those whose differential nodal drift sweeps them through it.

eco02_decay_benefit.caption: Does a 200 km kick change the compliance status of a 1 cm member of each cluster? (v5 R2 tension applied per cluster.)

eco02_viability_number.caption: THE viability-defining number: engagement opportunities that are both reachable and worth taking, per platform per decade.

eco02_clusters.caption: Modelled ≥1 cm membership of each major breakup cloud against the number one platform can actually reach in a decade, and whether a 200 km kick changes the compliance status of members at that altitude.

eco01_structural_tension.caption: The flux-versus-cost tension: fragments only drift into the firing cone if their altitude differs from the platform's, and that same difference is what makes them expensive to reach. The last column is constant -- see the invariant below.

eco01_dv_invariant.caption: Closed form: Delta-v per engagement = pi*v/(3.5*Omega_dot*T). Independent of the altitude band, so it cannot be tuned away. Validated against the structural table (107 m/s at Fengyun-1C, 10 yr) and against the tour simulation.

eco01_tour.caption: Simulated 10-year tour: engagements achieved against the Delta-v budget and the time each engagement takes.

eco01_propellant.caption: Propellant required for the tour Delta-v budget.

eco01_cadence.caption: Left: opportunities and cost are driven by the same altitude offset. Right: engagements achieved against Δv budget for a 10-year tour, with the niche threshold marked.

eco03_platform_cost.caption: Platform cost across dry mass, build cost per kg, launch price and fleet size (85% learning curve).

eco03_consumables.caption: Consumable mass and cost at the engagement counts ECO-1 actually delivers, against the counts the plan assumed.

eco04_architectures.caption: Cost per object for the small-debris tour (A) and the large-tracked-object variant (B), using the same kick physics.

eco04_value_model.caption: Avoided-collision value of removing one >=1 cm object, swept over the shell-overlap factor and the asset-value mix. The 'implied_losses_per_year' column is the model's own reality check: values far above ~1 conflict with the observed record of essentially zero confirmed >=1 cm debris losses, so the low overlap rows are the credible ones.

eco04_fleet_scaling.caption: Fleet scaling of architecture A with an 85% learning curve. Cost per object falls only as the learning curve allows, because engagements scale linearly with platforms.

eco04_economics.caption: Cost per object for the small-debris tour against the large-object variant, and the Î”v-per-engagement invariant that drives both. Sun-synchronous orbits, where the most valuable debris sits, have the slowest nodal regression and are therefore the most expensive to tour.

eco05_impulse_efficiency.caption: Mass that must be launched to deliver the same 51.8 m/s kick: FG01 projectile versus tug propellant. The tug figure includes accelerating the tug's own mass.

eco05_mission_scaled.caption: Full mission accounting with the platform scaled to carry its magazine -- the step ECO-4 omitted. Recoil delta-v is included: firing the magazine retrograde pushes the platform prograde.

eco05_crossover.caption: Cost per object for FG01 against an electric tug of equal platform cost servicing the same 10 objects, as target mass varies. Both carry the same tour Delta-v.

eco05_efficiency.caption: Left: cost per object against target mass for FG01 versus an electric tug of equal platform cost. Right: the kick's effective specific impulse against real propulsion systems. FG01 must launch 14% of the target's mass as tungsten, which is negligible for grams and decisive for tonnes.

las01_elevation_tension.caption: Ablation recoil points away from the illuminator, so the useful retrograde component vanishes at zenith where the optics are best, and peaks near the horizon where range, airmass and spot size are worst. The product has a shallow optimum that achieves neither.

las01_aperture_scaling.caption: Aperture and pulse energy needed to clear the ablation threshold at the optimum engagement geometry (7 deg past the meridian, ~46 deg elevation, 1150 km).

las02_angular_requirement.caption: Pointing requirement measured against the diffraction limit of each system's own sensing aperture. The margin column is the meaningful comparison: it is the headroom each system has against the physics of its own optics.

las02_detection.caption: Detection geometry and photon budget for a 1 cm, albedo-0.1 sphere. 'resolved_ratio' is target angular size divided by the diffraction limit: above 1 the target is an extended object whose centroid is directly measurable; below 1 it is an unresolved point source.

las02_cueing.caption: External orbit knowledge each system needs before an engagement can start. FG01 uses external cueing only to get within range of its own sensor, which then closes the loop; the laser must be handed a solution accurate to its spot radius at 1,186 km because it has no way to improve on it.

las02_degradation.caption: Delivered momentum as each system's aiming error grows, normalised to its own nominal tolerance. FG01 decays smoothly; the laser holds up and then goes to exactly zero when the fluence crosses the ablation threshold.

las02_repetition_counterpoint.caption: The honest counterpoint to the cliff argument: a laser firing hundreds of pulses averages over its own threshold, so the cliff degrades throughput rather than causing outright failure -- until the pointing error grows enough that the engagement no longer fits inside a pass.

las02_ablation_feedback.caption: The coupled ablation-and-estimation problem: each pulse changes the target's velocity, so an estimator that does not model its own effect walks off the target.

las02_point_ahead.caption: Point-ahead angle and the fractional accuracy with which it must be computed. The laser's lead is small but its tolerance is smaller; FG01's lead is large but its tolerance is larger.

las02_accuracy.caption: Left: delivered momentum against aiming error. FG01 decays smoothly because a partially-missed cloud still deposits mass; the laser goes to exactly zero once fluence drops below the ablation threshold. Right: each system's pointing requirement against the diffraction limit of its own aperture — FG01 works with two orders of magnitude of margin, the laser at the limit.

las03_laser_benchmarks.caption: High-energy repetitive nanosecond lasers. Only demonstrated systems set the benchmark (AM-9).

las03_technology_readiness.caption: Laser aperture and average power required to clear the ablation threshold on a 1 cm target at 900 km, against the highest demonstrated average power for repetitive nanosecond lasers.

las03_facility_throughput.caption: Ground-laser facility cost and throughput. Throughput is limited by the terminator window (the target must be sunlit while the site is dark for the tracking camera to work), by weather, and by acquisition overhead.

las03_catalogue_dependency.caption: Both systems depend on an external catalogue that does not yet exist for the 1 cm population. They depend on it to very different degrees.

las03_head_to_head.caption: Corrected head-to-head. The laser retains a large cost advantage; every accuracy and readiness metric favours FG01.

las03_target_size_scaling.caption: How the comparison scales with target size. FG01's mass penalty falls as 1/A_target and reaches 1; the laser's engagement time grows because a larger target needs proportionally more total impulse while the fluence per unit area is unchanged.

las03_readiness.caption: Left: average laser power required to clear the ablation threshold, against the highest demonstrated repetitive nanosecond laser. Right: each concept's prime hardware measured against demonstrated capability — FG01's coilgun sits far inside the envelope, the laser far outside it.

las04_vacuum_optics.caption: Space-based laser: spot size, pulse energy and pointing tolerance in vacuum. Without atmosphere the beam is diffraction-limited and the spot falls below the target size at short range, so essentially all energy lands.

las04_recoil_geometry.caption: Useful retrograde fraction of ablation recoil as a function of where the illuminator sits relative to the target. Recoil is along the line of sight, so only an illuminator AHEAD of the target along its velocity vector produces a retrograde push.

las04_dv_invariant.caption: Whether each architecture must transport itself to its targets. This, not the beam physics, is what decides small-debris economics.

las04_consumables.caption: Consumable comparison. A laser's magazine is effectively infinite: it converts sunlight. FG01 carries finite mass and must be resupplied.

las04_pointing.caption: Pointing tolerance of a space-based laser against FG01's, at matched engagement range. FG01 keeps a large advantage because its 'spot' is a physical cloud sized to the miss distance, while the laser's is set by diffraction.

las04_spaceborne.caption: Left: in vacuum a modest aperture drives the spot below the target size at short range, eliminating the ground laser's energy and technology problem. Right: but any architecture that must push retrograde must be co-orbital, and therefore pays the same Î”v per engagement â€” only the ground station escapes, by letting Earth's rotation do the transporting.
